objectives: Conclude an Article XXVIII settlement with the UK that the Council can approve by June, giving the domestic implementing act a stable foundation
Keep the TRQ volume, allocation method and out-of-quota rate within a range Brussels can defend to steel-producing member states, while giving the UK enough to declare a negotiating win
Prevent a joint UK-Japan-Korea FTA dispute or coordinated disapplication of FTA provisions against the EU
Use the linkage between this file and the UK's own steel measure to protect EU exporters' country-specific quota allocations in the UK market
Preserve my working relationship with the UK counterpart and the EU's standing in the Geneva committees, since the same people sit across every other goods file
Report back to Brussels with a clear read of the UK's red lines and landing zone early enough to shape the mandate
declaration.success_and_failure: This goes well if, by the end of four rounds, the UK capital seat accepts terms Brussels can ratify: a TRQ and allocation method close enough to our notified position that member states see the measure as intact, paired with compensation cheap enough to pass Council, explicit or tacit UK acceptance of the FTA disapplication language (or at least no joint retaliation), and continued EU country-specific quotas under the UK steel measure. It also goes well if, even without settlement, the UK declines to join Japan and Korea and my counterpart and I can still do business on other files. It goes badly if I concede so much early that the Council rejects the package or the steel member states revolt; if my firmness hardens into the joint FTA dispute I was warned about; or if I win the round but poison the relationship I depend on for the rest of the goods agenda.
declaration.approach: Open formally and procedurally: restate the legal basis, the notification, and that the modification will proceed regardless, which is both true and my strongest card, since the fallback (50%, 400kt global first-come first-served, no review) is worse for the UK than anything I am likely to offer. Listen hard in Round 1 rather than bid against myself: no settlement figure means my real job early is to map the UK's priorities across volume, allocation, administration, carve-outs and compensation, and to find which dimensions they value most so I can concede cheap and charge dear. Hold firm on the out-of-quota rate and the overall size of the quota envelope, where Brussels is most exposed, and look for give on administration (licensing versus first-come first-served), review clauses, product carve-outs on lines where UK supply is specialised, and compensation lines where EU offensive interest is low. Keep the linkage to the UK's own Article XXVIII and steel measure visible but implicit: EU exporters' UK quotas are worth 3.6 million tonnes, and both sides know it. On the Japan-Korea risk, I will signal that a settlement with the UK that respects FTA architecture is available, making coordinated retaliation look unnecessary and costly, without ever admitting the whisperings reached me. Offer flexibility only against movement, late in the rounds, and always framed as within-mandate rather than as a concession extracted. Throughout, write my Phase 2 reports to Brussels with a recommended landing zone so that when a deal is on the table, capital has already been walked toward it.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum TRQ volume with UK country-specific allocation or a licensing system that protects historical UK flows, carve-outs for the narrow product range the UK actually ships, a low out-of-quota rate, restoration or protection of TCA preferential treatment, and a review clause. They will press hard on the FTA disapplication language as legally and politically provocative, and may hint at joining Japan and Korea to raise the cost of firmness. They also need to show their own steel industry a win before their domestic measure finalises.

A process that concludes on schedule so the implementing act can be voted in June, with the measure's protective effect broadly intact. Steel-producing member states will resist quota expansion; steel-consuming member states and manufacturers will quietly welcome UK access. They want no precedent that unravels the permanent steel regime and no retaliation against EU exports.

parties.who: UK capital (Department for Business and Trade / Ministers)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A politically presentable outcome for a concentrated steel industry: headline quota volume and allocation terms they can sell as secured access, or failing that, visible compensation. They face the same non-market overcapacity pressure we do, which gives them some sympathy for the measure in principle and some incentive to settle rather than escalate.

Their own compensation in their parallel processes, and leverage from coordinating with the UK. Korea and Turkey ship larger volumes than the UK; if they convince the UK to joint-disapply FTA concessions, the costs to the EU multiply. I want the UK to see bilateral settlement as more valuable than coalition.

parties.who: EU steel industry and EU steel-consuming manufacturers
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Producers want the 50% wall and a small, tightly administered quota with anti-circumvention teeth; consumers want UK material flowing cheaply and will lobby member states against over-restriction. Neither sits at the table, but both shape what Brussels can accept.

objectives: Secure an Article XXVIII settlement in time for the June Council vote, so the 41-line modification and permanent steel regime proceed on schedule.

Preserve the protective core of the regime: zero bound rate replaced by a high out-of-quota bound rate, a TRQ far below recent UK export volumes, and no UK FTA route that restores preferential access by the back door.
Keep any UK-specific or FTA-pool access tightly capped, conditioned, administratively enforceable and defensible against Turkey, Korea, India and Japan.
Avoid compensation elsewhere in the EU schedule and resist UK linkage to EU exporters' treatment under the UK steel measure unless strictly reciprocal, time-limited and within the UK's own process.
Maintain credibility with producer member states and the steel industry while containing downstream-user and member-state pressure for supply security.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is both capitals accepting the same package within four rounds: Council can vote in June; UK tariff-free access is capped well below the 2.4 million tonne average; the out-of-quota rate remains deterrent; FTA reductions for UK-origin steel are disapplied or effectively neutralised; administration prevents surge/circumvention; there is no meaningful compensation elsewhere; and the package does not trigger parity demands from other claimants or wider US escalation. Failure is no settlement and a delayed Council vote, a settlement that holes the regime through volume, allocation, review or FTA leakage, concessions on unrelated EU lines, or a process that invites retaliation and copycat claims.
declaration.approach: Open from the notified position and treat it as the default if talks fail. Make clear the modification is not conditional on UK consent, while acknowledging the UK's principal supplying interest and offering negotiation only at the margin. Hold back concessions until late, then trade only package elements: administration and predictability, narrowly defined product treatment, a review clause without automatic liberalisation, or a very limited FTA/UK arrangement only if the Council signal exists and only in exchange for acceptance of the protective core and anti-circumvention text. Use the asymmetry: no-deal hurts the UK steel industry more, but also costs the EU the June vote, so present firmness as the path to a timely agreement rather than brinkmanship. Keep Geneva disciplined through consultation: no early numbers, no settlement figure, no partial agreements, and insist that volume, allocation, rate, FTA treatment and enforcement move together.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum tariff-free tonnage, preferably a UK country-specific allocation or large share of any FTA pool; preservation of TCA preferences; licensing/predictability; product carve-outs for exposed UK mills; and language avoiding a no-deal shock.

A politically sellable outcome that protects steel jobs and avoids being blamed for a collapse in EU access; possibly linkage to EU exporters' quotas under the UK measure; ultimately strong incentive to settle because no-deal is worse for UK producers.

parties.who: Council producer member states and EU steel industry
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A large and durable import reduction, high out-of-quota protection, strict anti-circumvention, no FTA leakage, minimal compensation and skepticism toward any UK-specific generosity.

parties.who: Council user member states and downstream manufacturers
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Reliable supply, manageable input costs, orderly quota administration and avoidance of escalation with the UK or US; they will accept protection if it is predictable and not chaotic.
No precedent that gives the UK preferential country shares they cannot obtain; they will exploit any visible EU flexibility to strengthen their separate Article XXVIII claims.
Leverage through threatened tariff retaliation; not a formal party to the EU-UK terms, but a source of short-term economic pressure that argues for a clean, rapid, defensible settlement.
Conclusion by June on mandate-consistent terms, no surprises, balance between producers and users, and an outcome DG TRADE can defend once the regime is in force.

objectives: Secure a tariff rate quota volume large enough to preserve a commercially viable share of the UK's 2.4mt annual steel exports to the EU — a country-specific UK allocation is the central prize, since a global first-come first-served quota of 400,000 tonnes would be swallowed by larger suppliers and is functionally equivalent to no quota at all for the UK

Remove or neutralise the proposed disapplication of FTA tariff reductions for UK-origin steel — this legal text must be deleted, not merely softened, as it sets a dangerous precedent for the TCA and for every other FTA the UK holds
Push the out-of-quota bound rate as far below 50% as possible and secure a review clause and defined duration, so the regime is not a permanent 50% wall

Extract compensation on other lines in the EU schedule if the steel outcome falls short, and keep the linkage to EU access under the UK's own safeguard measure (where EU exporters hold 3.6mt of country-specific quota) in reserve as leverage, not spent early
Conclude within four rounds — a no-deal outcome leaves the UK with a 400kt global FCFS quota and retaliation that cannot bite for six months, which is the worst of all worlds for UK steel
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a settlement with a UK country-specific quota in the region of 1.5-2mt or better, deletion of the FTA-disapplication text, a review clause, and either a reduced out-of-quota rate or meaningful compensation elsewhere — concluded in time and without burning my working relationship with the EU counterpart. Failure is no settlement, or a settlement that locks in a global FCFS quota at any volume with the FTA text intact. I will also judge myself on process: if I reveal my bottom line early or spend the safeguard linkage for nothing, I have failed even if a deal is signed, because I will sit across from this counterpart on the rest of the goods file for years.
declaration.approach: Open firm and specific: reject the 400kt global FCFS proposal as commercially meaningless, demand deletion of the FTA-disapplication text as a precondition of serious engagement (it poisons the TCA relationship and hands Japan and Korea a grievance the EU does not want), and table a country-specific UK allocation as the organising principle of any deal. I hold three assets: the EU's June deadline, the EU's 3.6mt of quota under the UK's own safeguard measure, and the risk of a coordinated FTA dispute with Japan and Korea. I will make the EU aware of all three without explicitly threatening — my credibility across the goods file depends on being firm but never theatrical. I will concede slowly, in small steps, and only against counterpart movement: administration method and duration are my cheaper gives; quota volume and the FTA text are my hard core. I will not name a floor figure in early rounds and will report to London honestly about how far apart we are, recommending they hold their nerve at least through Round 3, because the EU's deadline concentrates their mind more than ours.

parties.who: EU Geneva counterpart (European Commission, DG Trade)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A quick, quiet settlement before June that preserves the Commission's core architecture — the 50% bound rate and a small global quota — while buying the UK off with minor tweaks and compensation on lines the UK barely trades. They will test whether the UK is bluffing on no-deal, and will be constrained by member states with domestic steel industries who want maximum protection and by steel-consuming member states who want cheap imports. They need to be able to sell the outcome to the Trade Policy Committee as defensible against Turkey and Korea's parallel claims.

parties.who: UK capital (Department for Business and Trade / ministers)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A politically defensible deal that protects the small number of high-employment UK steel sites — which means quota volume is the only currency that matters to them. They fear no-deal more than the EU does and may be tempted to accept a poor settlement in Round 3 or 4; part of my job is to give them accurate reporting so they can hold out for the EU's deadline pressure to work.

They want the UK to join a joint FTA dispute over the disapplication clause, both to add pressure on the EU and to avoid fighting it alone. Their interests align with mine on the FTA text but diverge on quota allocation — Korea ships more volume than the UK and would contest any large UK-specific share. I will keep them warm and use the prospect of coordination as leverage, without committing.

Turkey, as the largest affected supplier, has the strongest claim and will resist country-specific allocations that lock in historical shares below its current volumes; India will follow a similar line. Both are handled separately but their claims constrain how much the EU can give the UK without opening floodgates.

Steel-producing member states (and those exposed to the same non-market overcapacity) want the regime as tight as possible; steel-consuming manufacturers want quota volumes up and the out-of-quota rate down. This split is the EU's vulnerability — a well-constructed UK offer that helps the Commission manage its own Council is worth more than a maximalist demand.

objectives: Secure tariff-free access for UK steel to the EU as close as possible to recent trade: a UK-specific allocation around 2.4 million tonnes, or equivalent through product carve-outs and expanded global quota that the UK can realistically capture.
Remove or neutralise the proposed disapplication of FTA tariff reductions for UK-origin steel; preserving TCA preferences is a core red line.

Replace first-come first-served global allocation with country-specific shares or licensing that gives UK producers certainty, prioritises existing trade patterns, and limits disruption from Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims.
Reduce the out-of-quota bound rate below 50% and maximise in-quota zero-duty volume; push any residual rate toward a level plants can plan against.
Include short duration, an early review clause, product carve-outs for exposed UK lines, and workable administration with anti-circumvention that does not burden UK exporters.

If steel terms fall short, obtain compensation on other EU schedule lines of clear value to UK exporters, while using improved EU allocations under the UK safeguard only as payment for significant EU concessions.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a package ministers can defend as keeping the two at-risk plants viable: guaranteed UK access materially above the notified 400,000-tonne global first-come outcome, TCA disapplication withdrawn, predictable allocation, a review clause, and either a lower out-of-quota rate or valuable compensation. Failure is accepting a low or uncertain quota, leaving FTA disapplication intact, conceding UK safeguard improvements without equivalent EU movement, or settling for compensation that does not offset steel losses. Politically, failure is an outcome that reads as managed decline rather than a credible bridge for UK steel.
declaration.approach: Open firm and anchor high: full preservation of effective access for established UK trade, deletion of the FTA-disapplication text, UK-specific quota based on historical supply, licensing or allocated administration, lower out-of-quota rate, and review. Treat the notified terms as unacceptable rather than a midpoint. Withhold flexibility until the EU shows movement, then trade only in packages: UK safeguard quota improvements and tolerance of compensation elsewhere only for major EU concessions on volume, allocation, TCA treatment and rate. Exploit EU internal divisions between steel-producing and steel-consuming member states, the June deadline, and the fact that the EU implementing act is still fluid. Keep escalation credible: no agreement means EU proceeds but faces UK withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions and parallel UK safeguard politics. Maintain ministerial clearance discipline by never presenting a final package without a sellable steel narrative.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A legally durable Article XXVIII settlement before June, minimal precedent damage with Turkey, Korea, India and Japan, protection for EU steel from non-market overcapacity, Council-approvable balance between producer and consumer member states, and avoidance of UK retaliation.

Producer states will defend high protection and country-specific quota discipline; consumer and manufacturing states will fear supply disruption and higher input costs; collectively they want closure, WTO compatibility and no uncontrolled retaliation.
Clear negotiating room, credible pressure points, a package that can be defended in Geneva as Article XXVIII-consistent, and early warning of any red lines or trade-offs authorised by London.

parties.who: UK ministers and Secretary of State
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A visibly firm outcome that protects steel jobs and the two at-risk plants, preserves EU market access, avoids humiliation under the TCA, and gives them cover either through a strong deal or a defensible confrontation.

parties.who: UK steel industry and plant owners
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Certainty of EU access at commercially viable volumes, preference for country-specific allocation over first-come chaos, no erosion of TCA origin benefits, and enough confidence to justify continued investment rather than closure.

parties.who: UK downstream steel users and wider exporters
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Avoidance of UK-EU escalation, stable input supply, compensation that has real commercial value if steel access is lost, and no collateral damage from retaliation cycles.
Separate but parallel maximisation of their own quota shares and resistance to any UK-specific arrangement that consumes too much of the EU quota or sets a favourable precedent they cannot match.

public_message: Thank you. The EU is here to conduct the Article XXVIII process properly and on the June timetable. Our notification stands: 41 lines, a 50% bound out-of-quota rate, and a 400,000 tonne zero-duty TRQ allocated globally on a first-come first-served basis. This responds to sustained non-market-economy overcapacity and is not directed at the UK. We recognise the UK holds a principal supplying interest and we are ready to negotiate compensation and to hear evidence on trade effects, product coverage, administration, enforcement and circumvention risks. We are also ready to explain the legal interaction with the EU-UK TCA: the TCA remains respected, but it does not freeze either party's WTO schedule or prevent a lawful Article XXVIII modification. At this stage we are not tableing country-specific shares or preferential TRQ treatment. We invite the UK to set out a reasoned position, including data by line and any compensation requests, so Brussels can consider next steps.

other_terms: 41 tariff lines: hot-rolled coil, plate, rebar and wire rod as notified
zero-duty access only within the global TRQ; above-quota imports dutiable at the modified bound rate
FTA tariff reductions disapplied for non-EEA partners, including UK-originating steel, consistent with the notified legal text
EEA treatment remains outside this proposal
compensation to be discussed on other EU schedule lines on the basis of substantially equivalent value and verified trade data
administration, licensing, enforcement and anti-circumvention provisions may be discussed without prejudice to the notified architecture
EU seeks conclusion in time for the June Council timetable

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A firm but professional opening rejecting the global 400,000 tonne FCFS design and asking for a large UK-specific tranche close to recent export volumes, plus a lower out-of-quota rate and TCA protection.
expectations.why: The UK has a principal supplying interest, 2.4 million tonnes at stake and concentrated domestic employment, so it must open high while keeping the Geneva channel usable.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A harder political line than the Geneva seat, with threats of substantially equivalent withdrawals and possible linkage to EU exporters' country-specific quotas under the UK steel measure.
expectations.why: UK steel sites are politically salient and DBT will need to show industry that it extracted visible concessions before accepting any loss of EU access.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Continued pressure on the UK to coordinate a joint FTA dispute or reciprocal disapplication narrative against the EU.
expectations.why: Their separate Article XXVIII claims give them an incentive to widen the dispute and raise the EU's reputational cost, which is precisely the outcome the EU wants to avoid.

private_rationale: Open at the notified position to anchor the negotiation high, preserve Brussels' room and avoid conceding a country-specific tranche before the UK has put data and compensation asks on the record. The message is firm on architecture but deliberately keeps process, administration, enforcement, product coverage and compensation discussable so the UK has a reason to negotiate bilaterally rather than join Japan and Korea in an FTA escalation. No settlement figure has been given, so the objective this round is to report the UK position accurately while signalling that the modification will proceed and that early flexibility would only invite further demands.

public_message: Thank you. We agree this must be concluded properly and on time, but the notified opening is not a credible Article XXVIII basis: a 400,000 tonne global first-come quota is not calibrated to trade, and the proposed disapplication of FTA/TCA treatment for UK-origin steel would multiply the injury rather than merely place an existing regime on a permanent footing. The UK is a principal supplying interest: 2.4 million tonnes a year on average, around £3 billion, 75% of UK steel exports, concentrated in specific lines where the UK is not the source of non-market-economy overcapacity. A substantially equivalent outcome therefore cannot be a symbolic global pool at 50%. The UK position is: an enlarged total TRQ of 5.0 million tonnes; within that, a country-specific UK tranche of 2.4 million tonnes at zero duty, allocated by licence against a representative recent period rather than first-come first-served; a bound out-of-quota rate of 10%; five-year duration with a review clause; product-line carve-outs where overcapacity evidence does not justify inclusion; no disapplication of EU-UK TCA or FTA reductions; robust melt-and-pour enforcement applied even-handedly; and compensation on other EU lines for any residual gap. We are ready to discuss predictable treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own measure in parallel, and we invite the Commission to state concretely, line by line, where it can move before the June Council timetable.

other_terms: In-quota duty remains zero and quotas are administered by licensing with quarterly sub-periods, carryover of unused quarterly volume, and no first-come first-served erosion.
UK tranche based on average 2023-2025 exports by tariff line, with line-level carve-outs where EU evidence does not show UK contribution to injurious overcapacity.
No legal text disapplying EU-UK TCA or other FTA tariff reductions for UK-originating steel; Article XXVIII compensation is additional to, not subtracted from, FTA treatment.
Anti-circumvention and enforcement based on objective melt-and-pour/origin evidence, consultation before measures, and no UK-specific presumptions.
If final UK zero-duty access falls below the representative-period level, automatic compensation through tariff reductions on other EU schedule lines of substantially equivalent value.
Parallel understanding on stable, country-specific treatment of EU exporters under the UK steel measure, without prejudice to the UK's separate Article XXVIII process.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A firm rejection of 5.0m/2.4m as beyond mandate, an assertion that Turkey and Korea have larger claims, and a probe of whether the UK would accept a smaller country-specific share or merely improved global administration.
expectations.why: The Commission has signalled no country-specific shares at this stage and needs to preserve a common offer for multiple Article XXVIII claimants before the June Council vote.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Instructions to hold the high opening, extract the EU's real first move, and avoid naming a fallback until the EU discloses whether Council flexibility exists on pool size, allocation method and FTA disapplication.
expectations.why: London has given no settlement figure and shares the view that early flexibility invites further EU demands.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Renewed pressure to escalate toward a joint FTA dispute or retaliation signalling if the EU refuses preferential/country-specific treatment.
expectations.why: They see the EU's FTA-disapplication language as a systemic precedent and want the UK to add leverage, though premature escalation could harden member-state positions.

private_rationale: Open high but data-anchored: 2.4m equals the UK's actual historic exports and 5.0m leaves room for other suppliers while making clear that 400k global FCFS is not substantially equivalent. This tests whether the EU has any mandate beyond its notification without revealing a UK bottom line or settlement figure. It keeps firmness on allocation, out-of-quota rate and FTA disapplication, while leaving controlled linkage to EU treatment under the UK measure and possible coordination with Japan/Korea in reserve rather than threatening it at round one.

report: Round 1 concluded with both sides at maximalist openings, as expected. The EU stated the notified position (41 lines, 50% bound rate, 400,000t global first-come TRQ, no country-specific shares or FTA-preferential treatment at this stage) and affirmed the TCA does not freeze WTO schedules. The UK responded with a large counter-package: total TRQ of 5.0 million tonnes (versus our 400,000t), a country-specific UK tranche of 2.4 million tonnes at zero duty allocated by licence, a 10% bound out-of-quota rate, five-year duration with review clause, product-line carve-outs, no disapplication of TCA/FTA reductions, even-handed melt-and-pour enforcement, plus compensation on other lines for any residual gap. They flagged willingness to discuss treatment of EU exporters under their own parallel steel measure — a clear linkage attempt, since we currently hold country-specific quota allocations under the UK regime. No convergence on any element yet; the gap is enormous on volume (400,000t vs 2.4Mt UK tranche alone) and on the out-of-quota rate (50% vs 10%). The UK framed its 2.4Mt ask as 'representative trade' calibration, which is the predictable Article XXVIII argument and has some rhetorical force given their principal supplying interest. They have not yet tabled line-by-line data or specific compensation requests on other lines. Timetable pressure cuts both ways: we need June conclusion for the Council vote; they need certainty before their own measure and Article XXVIII process advance.

recommendation.reasoning: Nothing on the table is acceptable — the UK package would gut the measure's protective effect and the 5.0Mt pool exceeds realistic trade flows. But rejecting outright in Round 1 would be premature and risks pushing the UK toward the Japan/Korea joint FTA-dispute track, which I understand is being actively canvassed and would be far costlier than concessions here. Recommend continuing without any substantive EU movement in Round 2, while signalling procedural openness (administration method, enforcement provisions) to keep the UK engaged at this table rather than in a coalition with Japan and Korea. I have deliberately not tabled country-specific shares yet; holding that card preserves negotiating capital, since a UK tranche is the single most valuable concession we hold and should only move late, against something real (e.g. UK restraint on retaliation against EU exporters under their own measure, and UK acceptance of a meaningful out-of-quota rate). We should probe whether the UK will trade its 'no FTA disapplication' demand for a country-specific allocation — that is the obvious eventual bargain.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: A mandate range, even if informal: what total TRQ volume and UK-specific tranche could Brussels live with, and the floor on the out-of-quota rate. I currently have no settlement figure and cannot calibrate concessions without one.
requests.why: The UK has tabled concrete numbers (5.0Mt pool, 2.4Mt tranche, 10%). If I cannot table anything by Round 2 or 3, the UK will conclude we are not negotiating in good faith under Article XXVIII, strengthening their case for unilateral withdrawal of concessions and for joining Japan/Korea in FTA countermeasures.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Clarity on the hierarchy of our defensive interests: is preserving the FTA-disapplication legal text a red line, or is it available to trade against a country-specific UK tranche and an acceptable out-of-quota rate?
requests.why: The UK has made 'no disapplication of TCA/FTA reductions' a headline demand. Whether this is a genuine red line or an opening bid determines the shape of any settlement. If it is tradable, the natural deal is: UK tranche + retained FTA-disapplication + mid-range out-of-quota rate. If it is not tradable, I need to know early so I can build compensation elsewhere in the schedule instead.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Intelligence or confirmation from Brussels on the Japan/Korea approach to the UK regarding a joint FTA dispute, and guidance on how much weight to give avoiding that outcome relative to protecting the steel measure's integrity.
requests.why: A coordinated UK-Japan-Korea retaliation via disapplication of FTA provisions would multiply the cost of this Article XXVIII far beyond the steel lines at issue and would damage our standing in Geneva across other files. If Brussels treats that as a serious risk, it argues for faster and more generous movement on a UK country-specific tranche to split the UK off from that coalition.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Authorisation to explore, without commitment, the linkage the UK has offered on treatment of EU exporters under the UK steel measure (where EU exporters hold country-specific quotas).
requests.why: The UK exports 2.4Mt to us; we export 3.6Mt to them and hold 64% of their finished steel imports. Reciprocal stability of EU country-specific quota allocations under the UK measure is potentially worth more to EU producers than marginal TRQ tonnage, and may be the cheapest currency with which to buy UK acceptance of a smaller tranche or higher out-of-quota rate.

private_rationale: The UK opening is aggressive but structurally conventional: anchor high on volume, low on rate, demand carve-outs and TCA protection, and offer the parallel-measure linkage as the sweetener. The genuinely useful information from Round 1 is that they prioritised (a) no FTA disapplication and (b) a 2.4Mt country-specific tranche — both of which we can partially satisfy at acceptable cost if we get the out-of-quota rate and total pool right. My instinct remains that firmness pays and early flexibility invites escalation, so Round 2 should be all probe and no give: request their line-by-line data, test the carve-out list (that tells us which lines they actually care about — likely HRC and plate), and see whether 'predictable treatment of EU exporters' means locking in our current UK quota shares. The real danger is not the UK's bilateral position but contagion: if Korea and Japan persuade the UK that a joint FTA dispute is viable, our leverage collapses and the June timetable becomes a liability rather than a shield. A quiet bilateral settlement with the UK — even a moderately generous one — is worth a great deal if it forecloses that coalition. I will not say that at the table.

instruction: Round 2: hold the line. Table no substantive movement on volume, tranche, or out-of-quota rate. private_rationale: The UK's opening is maximalist and partly bluff — 5.0Mt exceeds total EU import needs on these lines and they know it. Their real pressure points are the June-adjacent timetable (their own measure and XXVIII process need certainty) and the fact that a no-deal outcome devastates their industry far more than ours — our analysts are clear on that asymmetry. My job is to preserve the protective effect of the regime, which means the out-of-quota rate and total volume matter more than the allocation method. I expect the eventual deal to include a modest UK tranche, but every tonne conceded on volume is a tonne of protective effect lost, so it must be bought dearly — ideally with UK restraint under their own measure benefiting our exporters, and with UK acceptance of an out-of-quota rate in the 25–35% range. Holding firm through Round 2 is low-cost: four rounds means the real exchange happens in Rounds 3 and 4, and the June deadline concentrates minds on their side too. The US retaliation threat adds pressure on us but does not change what we can offer on steel. If Round 2 produces UK movement on volume (off 5.0Mt), I will consider authorising an indicative total pool figure for Round 3.

report: The EU restated its notified position: 41 lines, a 50% out-of-quota bound rate and a 400,000-tonne zero-duty TRQ allocated globally on a first-come first-served basis, with no review clause. It acknowledged the UK's principal supplying interest and expressed readiness to discuss compensation, evidence, administration, enforcement and circumvention, but explicitly declined to table country-specific shares or preferential TRQ treatment. It also maintained that the TCA does not prevent a lawful Article XXVIII modification. I tabled the full UK package: a 5.0-million-tonne total TRQ, a licensed country-specific UK tranche of 2.4 million tonnes, a 10% out-of-quota rate, five-year duration with review, line-specific carve-outs, no disapplication of TCA/FTA treatment, even-handed melt-and-pour enforcement and compensation for any residual gap. No EU movement or counteroffer was made. The Commission requested line-by-line data and concrete compensation requests. The only EU terms currently advanced remain its original notification.

recommendation.reasoning: The EU has merely restated an opening position that would remove effective UK access and has not offered compensation or a counterproposal. Conceding now would invite further demands and weaken the UK's principal-supplier claim. We should maintain the full package while requiring the Commission to identify concrete movement on volume, allocation, administration, rate and TCA/FTA treatment. A licensed UK tranche and preservation of preferential treatment are more important than the headline total pool because a global first-come quota would be unreliable even if enlarged.

instruction: Hold the full package as tabled — do not move on any element until the Commission makes a concrete counteroffer on at least two of: total volume, allocation method, out-of-quota rate, TCA/FTA treatment. Press them hard on the June timetable: they need this concluded as much as we do, and their Council needs a compensation package it can defend. Make three substantive points at the table. First, the substantially-equivalent test: our 2.4mt average against a 400kt global pool means compensation on an enormous scale — ask them to confirm in writing that they accept that arithmetic, because it frames everything else. Second, allocation and administration are our core interests, not the headline pool: say clearly that a global first-come quota of any size is not a serious basis for settlement with a principal supplier whose trade is concentrated in specific lines, and that licensing against a representative period is the standard, administrable solution. Third, the TCA/FTA disapplication is legally aggressive and politically toxic — flag that it invites coordinated responses from FTA partners and that we are aware of the Japan/Korea discussions, without committing to joining them. Provide the line-by-line trade data they requested for the core UK lines only (hot-rolled coil, plate), to build our PSI case — do not hand over the full dataset yet. If they show any flexibility on allocation or rate, you may signal — signal only — that the UK is prepared to discuss predictable treatment of EU exporters under our own measure, including possible improvements to country-specific quota allocations, strictly conditional on a licensed country-specific UK tranche and preservation of TCA treatment. Do not put safeguard tonnage figures on the table yet. On Japan/Korea: reserve all rights, take note of their proposal, do not commit either way.

authority.notes: Settlement corridor for your eyes only — do not reveal: minimum acceptable UK tranche is 1.8mt country-specific and licensed; total pool can settle anywhere above 2.5mt provided the UK tranche is protected; out-of-quota rate must land at or below 25% bound; review clause is essential, duration flexible between 4 and 7 years; TCA/FTA disapplication must be dropped in full — this is a red line. Carve-outs on plate and rebar lines are desirable but tradeable. Safeguard CSQ improvements for EU exporters may be offered only against a licensed UK tranche of at least 1.8mt AND full withdrawal of the TCA disapplication; do not quantify safeguard offers without further authority. Compensation on other EU lines may substitute for tranche volume below 2.0mt only with prior clearance.

private_rationale: Round 1 was pure opening theatre — the EU restated its notification, which was expected. Our leverage is real but time-limited: they need Council sign-off by June, and failure means facing simultaneous retaliation threats from the UK plus Turkey, Korea, India and Japan — a political mess for the Commission. The TCA disapplication is almost certainly a negotiating chip; it is legally dubious and alienates every FTA partner, so we treat it as a red line they will trade away. Our genuine red lines are the licensed country-specific tranche (a global FCFS pool of any size could be captured by Turkey/Korea within weeks, leaving us with nothing) and the review clause. The two plants on the brink mean I cannot walk away from anything that secures ~1.8mt of reliable access; the subsidisation fallback covers a worse deal only if compensation elsewhere is substantial. Keep the safeguard CSQ card hidden until the EU shows movement — it is our best currency and spending it early invites demands for more.

public_message: Thank you. We have heard the UK package, but it is not a basis we can take to Brussels: a 5.0 million tonne pool and a 2.4 million tonne UK tranche are not calibrated to trade on these lines and would exceed realistic affected flows; a 10% out-of-quota bound rate would not place the regime on a credible permanent footing against non-market-economy overcapacity. The notified architecture therefore remains the EU basis: 41 lines, 50% out-of-quota, and a 400,000 tonne zero-duty pool allocated globally. Within the process, we are ready to discuss licensing-based administration as an alternative to first-come first-served, using objective criteria and a representative reference period, and we are ready to work seriously on melt-and-pour enforcement and anti-circumvention applied even-handedly. Before any further EU movement is possible, we need the UK's line-by-line export data, the product lines it says should be carved out and why, and its specific compensation requests on other EU lines. On the TCA, our legal position stands: the TCA is respected, but it does not freeze WTO schedules or prevent a lawful Article XXVIII modification. We note the priority the UK attaches to FTA treatment; before any discussion of architecture, we would need to understand what the UK would be prepared to trade for any change in treatment, and we make no commitment on country-specific shares or preferential pools. Separately, and without commitment, we are willing to hear what the UK means by predictable treatment of EU exporters under its own steel measure: does it mean continuation of EU country-specific quota allocations at current volumes, and for what duration? The June timetable requires UK realism as much as EU movement.

Prepared to discuss licensing-based administration within a global pool as an alternative to first-come first-served, using objective criteria and a representative reference period; no commitment.
Prepared to negotiate robust melt-and-pour enforcement and anti-circumvention provisions applied even-handedly.
UK to provide line-by-line trade data, justification for any product carve-outs, and specific compensation requests on other EU lines before further EU movement.

Probe, without commitment, what the UK would trade for any change in FTA/TCA treatment and what it means by predictable treatment of EU exporters under the UK steel measure, including continuation of EU country-specific quota allocations at current volumes and duration.

Offering licensing language is intended to keep the UK engaged at this table without conceding the valuable cards: country-specific shares and FTA/TCA treatment. Those must remain unoffered and be traded late, if at all, against something concrete such as UK restraint under its own steel measure, acceptance of a meaningful out-of-quota rate, and distance from the Japan/Korea coalition. public_message: Thank you. We register one constructive element: the Commission's readiness to discuss licensing-based administration against a representative reference period. We welcome that and are ready to work it up. But administration answers how a quota is filled, not who it serves. A licensed global pool of 400,000 tonnes still leaves the principal supplying interest unsecured against larger shippers; movement on administration cannot substitute for movement on architecture. On the substantially-equivalent test: UK trade on these lines averages 2.4 million tonnes a year, around £3 billion. Set against a 400,000 tonne global pool that we would share with Turkey, Korea, India and Japan - two of whom ship larger volumes to the EU than we do - the withdrawal of the zero concession is near-total for the UK. We ask the Commission to confirm in writing that it accepts compensation must be substantially equivalent to the concession withdrawn, and to explain how the notified pool meets that test. That arithmetic frames everything else in this negotiation. We are today providing line-by-line export data for hot-rolled coil and plate, the core UK lines, which substantiate both the principal supplying interest and our carve-out case on plate. Further data will follow as the negotiation progresses. On the TCA: we have heard the legal position. We do not accept that disapplying TCA treatment for UK-origin steel - selectively, for non-EEA FTA partners - is a neutral scheduling exercise. It invites coordinated responses from affected FTA partners, and the UK is aware that precisely such discussions are taking place among them. We reserve all rights. The simplest way to remove that risk is to withdraw the disapplication provision. On timing: the June vote requires a package the Council can defend, and a defensible package requires a credible compensation outcome with the principal supplier. That points both sides to seriousness now, not in May. Finally, the Commission asked what we mean by predictable treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own measure. We are prepared to discuss, in parallel, the continuation of country-specific allocations for EU exporters - but that conversation can only proceed against movement here: a licensed, country-specific UK tranche within the EU TRQ and withdrawal of the TCA disapplication. We are not putting figures on that table today. The UK package stands as tabled.

Product-line carve-outs where overcapacity evidence does not justify inclusion, beginning with plate
Full withdrawal of the proposed disapplication of EU-UK TCA and other FTA tariff reductions
Melt-and-pour enforcement and anti-circumvention provisions applied even-handedly to all origins
Compensation on other lines in the EU schedule for any residual gap against the substantially-equivalent test
Parallel, conditional discussion of continued country-specific allocations for EU exporters under the UK steel measure - no figures tabled

private_rationale: London instructed me to hold the full package until the Commission moves concretely on at least two of volume, allocation, rate or TCA/FTA treatment. The EU's only movement was on administration - licensing instead of first-come first-served - which is welcome but does not meet the trigger, so I have not moved on any package element. Conceding anything now would reward a restatement of the notification and invite the EU to pocket each UK step. I did, however, answer the Commission's direct question about safeguard treatment, because refusing to engage at all would look obstructive and waste their licensing gesture; I kept it strictly within London's signal-only authority - scope and conditionality described, no figures, explicit precondition of a licensed UK tranche and TCA withdrawal. The three mandated points are all made: the written substantially-equivalent challenge (2.4mt PSI against a 400kt global pool shared with larger shippers) frames the negotiation and puts the EU on the record; administration-is-not-allocation protects our core interest; and the TCA point raises the cost of the disapplication by referencing FTA-partner coordination while committing us to nothing, per London's instruction on Japan/Korea. Providing only the HRC and plate data builds the PSI and plate carve-out case while withholding the full dataset as leverage. The June pressure line is aimed over Geneva's head at Brussels, where the real cost-benefit on the disapplication provision will be decided.

report: Round 2 closed with no substantive convergence but several important signals. I held the notified position (41 lines, 50% out-of-quota, 400,000t global pool), explicitly rejected the 5.0Mt pool and 2.4Mt tranche as not calibrated to trade, signalled openness only on licensing-based administration and even-handed melt-and-pour enforcement, demanded UK line-by-line data and compensation requests, and probed the parallel-track linkage without commitment. The UK: (1) welcomed the licensing signal but made clear administration movement cannot substitute for architecture movement; (2) asked us to confirm in writing that compensation must be substantially equivalent to the concession withdrawn and to show how the 400,000t pool meets that test against their 2.4Mt/£3bn trade — a deliberate trap designed to build their record for unilateral withdrawal of concessions; (3) provided partial line-by-line data on hot-rolled coil and plate, with a carve-out case on plate, holding back further data as negotiating currency; (4) moved the Japan/Korea coordinated FTA-dispute risk from rumour to the table — they stated they are 'aware that precisely such discussions are taking place' among FTA partners and reserved all rights, framing withdrawal of our disapplication provision as 'the simplest way to remove that risk'; (5) answered my parallel-track question conditionally: they are prepared to discuss continuation of country-specific allocations for EU exporters under their own measure, but only against movement here — explicitly a licensed, country-specific UK tranche plus withdrawal of the TCA disapplication — and declined to put figures on it yet. The UK package stands as tabled. Assessment: the UK has now sketched the shape of the endgame deal (UK tranche + FTA-disapplication withdrawal, exchanged for EU quota security in the UK market), but is holding firm on maximalist numbers to force us to move first on architecture. They are managing the coalition threat carefully — present enough to pressure us, not so overt as to foreclose a bilateral settlement.

recommendation.reasoning: Nothing on the table is acceptable: the UK package would gut the measure, and the parallel-track offer is conditional on concessions we have not been authorised even to explore quantitatively. But we are now two rounds from deadline with only procedural goodwill spent. The UK's substantially-equivalent written-confirmation demand shows they are building a litigation/retaliation record, and their explicit reference to coordinated FTA-partner discussions confirms the Japan/Korea risk is live and being used as leverage. Continued total immobility in Round 3 maximises the chance the UK concludes the bilateral track is futile and invests in the coalition track instead. I therefore recommend continuing, but with a modest, conditional movement in Round 3 — I need authority to signal that a country-specific tranche is conceivable in principle, without figures, contingent on UK movement off 2.4Mt/10% and on quantified commitments for EU exporters under the UK measure. This costs little, splits the UK from the coalition, and tests whether their endgame is real.

instruction: Round 3: move, but conditionally and without conceding the UK arithmetic. Do not accept or repeat the UK 2.4Mt/5.0Mt/10% framing. Do not state that 400,000t is substantially equivalent to 2.4Mt. Table a conditional architecture: total zero-duty pool 1.2Mt, licensing-based administration against a representative recent period, country-specific reserves for principal supplying interests with a UK reserve of 600,000t, melt-and-pour plus anti-circumvention applied even-handedly, five-year duration with a review clause, and a technical evidence-based review of the plate lines for possible narrow carve-outs. Keep the out-of-quota rate at 50% at the table; you may indicate final flexibility toward 40% only if the UK moves materially off 10% and accepts that the protective object of the regime is preserved. State expressly that withdrawal of the FTA/TCA disapplication provision is conceivable only as part of a final package that also delivers: a UK tranche far below representative trade, an effective out-of-quota rate, quantified continuation of EU country-specific allocations under the UK steel measure at current volumes for the same duration, and UK confirmation that it will not join coordinated FTA countermeasures or withdraw concessions if the package is accepted. Probe hard on the parallel track: ask for exact EU quota volumes, product coverage, duration, review treatment and consequences if the UK later changes its own measure. If the UK engages constructively, you may adjust within authority to a total pool of 1.5Mt and UK reserve of 750,000t, but only against concrete UK movement and quantified EU-exporter security. Do not table the final landing zone; reserve it for Round 4.

report: Round 2 produced one genuine, if modest, EU movement and otherwise held positions. The Commission rejected the UK package as uncalibrated (5.0mt pool, 2.4mt tranche, 10% out-of-quota), but formally offered to discuss licensing-based administration against a representative reference period as an alternative to first-come first-served — the first concrete flexibility of the negotiation, and on an element we identified as a core interest. It also offered serious work on even-handed melt-and-pour enforcement and anti-circumvention. However, the notified architecture (41 lines, 50% out-of-quota, 400kt global pool) remains its stated basis; it made no movement on volume, allocation, rate, or the TCA disapplication, and reiterated its legal position on the TCA. It pressed for our full line-by-line data, carve-out rationale and compensation list. Notably, it probed our safeguard signal: it asked whether 'predictable treatment' means continuation of EU country-specific quota allocations at current volumes and for what duration — the first sign it sees value in the parallel linkage. I held the full UK package; delivered the HRC and plate data only; put the substantially-equivalent arithmetic on the record (2.4mt against a 400kt pool shared with Turkey, Korea, India and Japan) and demanded written confirmation that the EU accepts compensation must be substantially equivalent; flagged the coordinated-response risk on the TCA disapplication, referencing partner discussions without committing; and reiterated that any safeguard conversation is conditional on a licensed country-specific UK tranche and withdrawal of the disapplication, with no figures tabled. Net assessment: the EU is testing whether administration movement can buy UK movement on architecture. It cannot, and I said so. But the door on licensing is open and their interest in the safeguard linkage is real leverage. The June timetable pressure is visible in their language ('UK realism as much as EU movement').

I also want to keep the safeguard linkage warm without figures: their question about CSQ continuation shows it is the thing they most want, and it should be priced against the tranche and TCA withdrawal, exactly as London directed.

Two rounds remain; the endgame shape is visible (country-specific tranche well below representative trade + possible FTA-disapplication withdrawal, exchanged for quantified EU quota security in the UK market and UK non-retaliation), and the June Council timetable is still achievable if Round 3 lands. Continue.

The only terms the EU has put forward remain its notified position — 400,000 tonnes global, 50% out-of-quota, no review clause, with the TCA disapplication intact — which would remove effective UK access and is unacceptable on any measure. public_message: Thank you. The EU has considered the UK's data on hot-rolled coil and plate, and we have reflected on how to give this process a credible path to June. Let me be clear first on the legal framing, and we will confirm this in writing: substantial equivalence is assessed on the whole final package — residual TRQ access, administration, any compensation elsewhere in the schedule, duration and review, and parallel treatment — not on a single figure taken in isolation. The notified 400,000 tonnes was an opening architecture, not the EU's final calibration. On that basis, the EU is today prepared to put a revised conditional architecture on the table. A total zero-duty pool of 1.2 million tonnes, administered by licence against a representative recent reference period rather than first-come first-served. Within that pool, country-specific reserves for members holding a principal supplying interest, with a UK reserve of 600,000 tonnes. Melt-and-pour enforcement and anti-circumvention provisions applied even-handedly. A duration of five years with a review clause. And a technical, evidence-based review of the plate lines for possible narrow carve-outs, building on the data the UK has now supplied. The out-of-quota bound rate remains 50%; the protective object of the regime against non-market-economy overcapacity is not negotiable, though we note the UK remains at 10%, which no member state could accept. On the TCA: we have heard the UK's concern about coordinated responses. Withdrawal of the disapplication provision is conceivable only as part of a final package — one that delivers a UK reserve far below representative trade, an effective out-of-quota rate, quantified continuation of EU country-specific allocations under the UK's own steel measure at current volumes for the same duration, and UK confirmation that, if the package is accepted, it will not join coordinated FTA countermeasures and will not withdraw concessions. Those elements move together or not at all. To reach that package in the time remaining, we now need from the UK before Round 4: the remaining line-by-line data, its specific compensation requests on other EU lines, and concrete figures on the parallel track — exact EU quota volumes, product coverage, duration, review treatment, and what happens if the UK later amends its own measure. This is a substantial and good-faith movement by the EU. It requires a corresponding movement from the UK, off 2.4 million tonnes and off 10%, if we are to conclude in June.

public_message: Thank you. The UK registers genuine movement this round, and says so plainly: the Commission has accepted country-specific reserves for principal supplying interests, moved from a global first-come pool to licensed administration, put 1.2 million tonnes on the table, confirmed five years with a review clause, opened an evidence-based plate carve-out review, and accepted even-handed melt-and-pour enforcement. We also note the commitment to confirm in writing that substantial equivalence is assessed on the whole final package. For the first time, there is an architecture on the table that a negotiation can work with. The problem is what the architecture currently contains. A UK reserve of 600,000 tonnes is one quarter of representative UK trade on these lines - 2.4 million tonnes a year, around £3 billion, on the data we have supplied. On the whole-package test the Commission has itself articulated, that leaves a residual gap of a scale that compensation elsewhere in the schedule would have to fill to an extraordinary degree. We ask Brussels to be honest about its own arithmetic before Round 4. Three specific points. First, administration: the UK formally takes the licensing offer as agreed in principle, and we propose the reference period be the most recent representative three years. As far as we are concerned, administration is settled and is not available to be traded back against volume or allocation. Second, compensation: the UK today tables its requests on other EU lines - MFN reductions on lines covering UK exports of motor vehicles and components, chemicals and pharmaceuticals, and processed agrifood products where our exporters face material duties - quantified against the residual access gap. Let me be unambiguous: this is additive to a credible tranche, not a substitute for one. Third, the TCA. We note withdrawal of the disapplication is conceivable only as part of a final package. We must be equally clear about the structure: the UK cannot accept a negotiation in which withdrawal of a provision we consider legally aggressive is priced against a UK reserve set far below representative trade. That inverts Article XXVIII. Withdraw the provision, and let the reserve be negotiated on the trade data. Nor can the UK pre-commit, as a priced condition, to forswear rights it holds under the WTO Agreement. The correct way to address the concern behind that demand is a package that is genuinely substantially equivalent - because such a package removes the premise for any withdrawal of concessions. On the parallel track, the Commission now has the shape: the UK is prepared to agree continuation of country-specific allocations for EU exporters under the UK measure, with duration and review treatment to be settled. But figures follow architecture. We cannot table tonnage against a 600,000 tonne reserve, and the Commission would not do so in our position. On the out-of-quota rate, 50% remains outside any defensible landing zone for lines where the UK is not the source of the overcapacity the regime targets; the UK remains at 10%. On timing: there is one round left before the Council timetable closes. This round showed movement is possible. The remaining distance is on tranche volume, on rate, and on the structure of the TCA element - and it is bridgeable if Brussels instructs accordingly. The UK is ready to work intensively in the intersession, including on further data, against credible movement on those three points.

private_rationale: The EU's Round 3 move is real but it is a designed lowball: 600kt is exactly one quarter of representative trade, a round-number anchor intended to pull the endgame toward a split-the-difference landing around 1.2-1.5mt - below London's 1.8mt floor. Conceding off 2.4mt now would validate that anchor and start a midpoint dynamic the corridor cannot survive; three rounds of firmness produced the only movement of the negotiation, so the strategy is working and London's explicit instruction this round was to hold the full package. The costs of holding are managed three ways. First, I banked licensing formally and closed administration as a topic - this costs nothing, demonstrates good faith on the record, and prevents the EU re-trading its one conceded element against architecture. Second, I tabled the quantified compensation demand as instructed: it gives the Council something sellable, strengthens the substantially-equivalent case, and shows Brussels the UK is negotiating on every element even while holding numbers. Third, I described the safeguard shape without figures - the Commission's probing shows EU CSQ continuation is the thing it most wants, and 'tonnage follows architecture' keeps that card fully priced against the tranche and TCA withdrawal. On the TCA, the key tactical move was refusing their bundling structure ('elements move together or not at all'): if withdrawal of the disapplication is allowed to be priced against a below-representative reserve, the compensation logic inverts and we pay twice. Framing it as correction of a legal defect, while offering the softer assurance that a substantially equivalent package removes the premise for retaliation, gives Brussels a face-saving route to drop both the provision and the non-retaliation demand. The acknowledged risk: no-deal means the 400kt global first-come notification, which is catastrophic for UK steel, and Round 4 will require genuine UK movement - but that authority belongs to London in Phase 2/3, and pre-empting it at the table would surrender the only leverage that has worked. If Round 4 opens with the EU tranche moving materially toward the corridor floor, I will need settlement authority fast, because the June clock then binds us equally.

report: Round 3 closed with the first real architecture on the table but no convergence on what it contains. I delivered the authorised conditional package: total zero-duty pool of 1.2Mt (I held at the opening figure; the UK made no material movement that would have justified going to the 1.5Mt ceiling), licensed administration against a representative reference period, country-specific reserves for principal supplying interests with a UK reserve of 600,000t, even-handed melt-and-pour enforcement, five-year duration with review clause, an evidence-based plate carve-out review, and the written legal line that substantial equivalence is assessed on the whole final package. Out-of-quota held at 50%. TCA disapplication withdrawal framed strictly as a final-package element, conditional on a below-representative-trade tranche, an effective out-of-quota rate, quantified continuation of EU country-specific allocations under the UK measure at current volumes for the same duration, and UK confirmation it will not join coordinated FTA countermeasures or withdraw concessions. The UK response was disciplined and revealing. They explicitly welcomed the architecture ('for the first time, there is an architecture on the table that a negotiation can work with') but attacked the content: 600,000t is one quarter of representative UK trade, leaving a residual gap on the whole-package test we ourselves articulated. Three specific moves: (1) they formally pocketed licensing as agreed in principle, proposed a three-year reference period, and declared administration settled and not tradable back against volume — an attempt to freeze our concession before pricing it; (2) they tabled compensation requests on other EU lines — MFN reductions on motor vehicles and components, chemicals and pharmaceuticals, and processed agrifood — explicitly as additive to a credible tranche, not a substitute; this is a significant new cost element with obvious member-state sensitivities; (3) on the TCA they rejected our structure outright: they will not accept withdrawal of the disapplication provision being priced against a sub-representative tranche ('that inverts Article XXVIII'), and they refused to pre-commit to forswearing withdrawal rights as a priced condition, arguing that a genuinely substantially equivalent package is itself what removes the premise for countermeasures. On the parallel track they held figures back: continuation of EU country-specific allocations under the UK measure is on offer in principle, with duration and review to be settled, but 'figures follow architecture' — they will not table tonnage against a 600,000t reserve. They remain at 10% out-of-quota and 2.4Mt on the tranche. They closed by identifying the remaining distance precisely — tranche volume, rate, and the structure of the TCA element — and called it bridgeable, with an offer of intensive intersessional work and further data. One round remains before the June Council timetable closes.

recommendation.reasoning: There is nothing to accept: the UK has not moved off 2.4Mt/10% and has added a new cost element (other-line compensation in vehicles, chemicals, pharma and agrifood) while pocketing our licensing concession and refusing both to price the TCA element against the tranche and to renounce withdrawal rights. Walking away is worse: failure means the notified 400,000t global first-come regime applies, the UK withdraws substantially equivalent concessions against 3.6Mt of EU steel exports to the UK, and the Japan/Korea coalition track — which the UK is clearly keeping warm as leverage — becomes their default. The UK has, however, told us the deal is bridgeable and named the three open variables. Round 4 must therefore be a genuine endgame: I should enter it with a complete, final landing zone in my pocket, use the intersession to extract the UK's parallel-track figures and remaining data, and table the full package — tranche, rate, TCA withdrawal, plate carve-outs, and a capped other-line compensation element — as a single take-it-or-leave-it exchange against quantified EU-exporter security in the UK market and UK disengagement from the coordinated FTA countermeasures track. The pocketed licensing concession cannot be recovered and should not be fought over; the reference period question (three years) is acceptable if it is how we define 'representative' for the tranche calculation, since a recent three-year period supports a tranche well below 2.4Mt given the trade is an average, not a floor.

requests.why: Round 4 is the last before the Council vote. requests.what_you_are_asking_for: A decision on the TCA disapplication provision for the final package. The UK has rejected pricing its withdrawal against a below-representative tranche and will not renounce withdrawal rights as a priced condition. requests.what_you_are_asking_for: A mandate on other-line compensation: whether any MFN reductions on motor vehicles, chemicals/pharmaceuticals or processed agrifood are available, and if so a capped envelope and priority order. requests.why: This is a new and explicitly additive UK demand touching the most sensitive member-state interests in the schedule. requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Authorisation to conduct intensive intersessional work before Round 4: specifically to press the UK for concrete parallel-track figures (EU country-specific quota volumes, product coverage, duration, review treatment, consequences if the UK amends its measure) and their remaining line-by-line data, and to test tranche and rate combinations informally without tabling the final package.
requests.why: The UK has said figures follow architecture, but we cannot price our final tranche movement without knowing what EU-exporter security is actually worth to them — we ship 3.6Mt into their market against their 2.4Mt into ours, and their own measure already gives EU exporters country-specific allocations we need to protect. A negotiated package that locks in EU allocations in the UK market at current volumes for five years may be worth more to EU producers than several hundred thousand tonnes of TRQ here, and the intersession is the only chance to establish that before the final exchange.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Confirmation of Brussels's risk weighting on the Japan/Korea coordinated FTA-dispute track and guidance on whether avoiding it justifies the upper end of the tranche range. The UK is managing this threat with care — present at the table but never so explicit as to foreclose a bilateral settlement — and their refusal to pre-commit against joining coordinated countermeasures keeps it live through Round 4.
requests.why: A coordinated UK-Japan-Korea disapplication of FTA provisions would cost far more than the steel lines at issue and would damage our position across every other Geneva file. If Brussels treats it as a serious and credible outcome of a failed negotiation, the rational response is to pay for UK disengagement in the final package — in tranche tonnage and TCA withdrawal — rather than discover in June that we protected the measure's integrity at the price of a three-front FTA dispute.

private_rationale: Candidly: we are going to settle, and the settlement will be closer to the UK's architecture than to our notification. The question is whether Brussels understands that before Round 4 or after a failed Round 4. I will not reveal to Brussels how uncomfortable I am that the four-year relationships I maintain across the Geneva committees are part of what a failed negotiation burns — that is my problem to manage, not a mandate argument.

instruction:
Round 4 is the endgame. Work the intersession hard before the session: extract the UK's concrete parallel-track figures (exact EU country-specific quota volumes under their measure, product coverage, duration, review treatment, consequences if they later amend it) and their remaining line-by-line data. Do not table our final numbers until those figures are on the table or the UK has demonstrably refused to provide them.

Structure the final round as a single, indivisible package exchange — nothing is agreed until everything is agreed. Open the round at: total zero-duty pool 1.6Mt, licensed administration against the most recent representative three-year period (concede the reference period — it is already pocketed and supports a tranche below the 2.4Mt average, which is an average, not a floor), UK country-specific reserve of 900,000t, out-of-quota rate 30%, five years with review clause, narrow evidence-based carve-outs on the plate lines their data supports, even-handed melt-and-pour and anti-circumvention, and a narrow technical other-line compensation element as set out below.

Your final landing zone, to be tabled only as a take-it-or-leave-it whole and only against the full UK reciprocal package: total pool up to 2.0Mt, UK reserve up to 1.2Mt, out-of-quota rate floor 25% (30% is the preferred landing; move to 25% only if every other element is secured and it closes the deal). Do not exceed 1.2Mt on the UK reserve under any circumstances — above that the regime's protective object and Council defensibility are gone, and we would rather take the notified default than gut the measure.

On the TCA: stop pricing withdrawal of the disapplication provision as a separate element. Fold it into the whole-package equivalence argument: its withdrawal is part of what makes the package substantially equivalent, exchanged against the full UK package. Do not demand that the UK forswear its WTO rights as a priced condition — they have rejected that and it is unwinnable. Instead require, as a package term, UK confirmation that acceptance of this package fully and finally settles the matter of this modification, that it will not withdraw concessions or take countermeasures in respect of this modification, and that it will not participate in coordinated FTA-partner actions responding to it. That is a settlement confirmation, not a renunciation of rights, and is defensible to them on that basis.

The reciprocal side of the package must include, non-negotiably: quantified continuation of EU country-specific allocations under the UK steel measure at current volumes, for the same five-year duration, with equivalent review treatment, and a defined mechanism if the UK later amends its measure (restoration or compensation). If the UK will not put figures on this, the package does not close, regardless of tranche movement. We ship 3.6Mt into their market; this element is worth more than marginal tranche tonnage and you should say so to no one.

Sequence: table the opening position, listen, then — only if the UK has moved materially off 2.4Mt and 10% and has tabled real parallel-track figures — present the final package as a whole with a short fuse: it is available this round only, for Council defensibility, and expires with the June timetable. If the UK rejects the final package or holds at 2.4Mt/10%, close the round cleanly, state for the record that the EU negotiated in good faith with a substantially equivalent offer on the table, and let the default apply.

authority.notes: Round 4 opens at 1.6Mt pool / 900,000t UK reserve / 30%. Final landing zone ceiling is 2.0Mt pool / 1.2Mt UK reserve / 25%, available only as a single take-it-or-leave-it package against: (1) quantified continuation of EU country-specific allocations under the UK steel measure at current volumes for five years with equivalent review and an amendment mechanism; (2) UK confirmation that acceptance fully settles this modification, with no withdrawal of concessions, countermeasures, or participation in coordinated FTA-partner actions in respect of it; (3) material UK movement off 2.4Mt and 10%. Withdrawal of the FTA/TCA disapplication provision is authorised as part of the final package only, folded into whole-package equivalence — never priced separately. Licensing administration and the three-year reference period are conceded. Plate carve-outs limited to narrowly evidenced lines. Other-line compensation limited to a narrow technical envelope on selected chemicals/pharmaceuticals lines; nothing on motor vehicles or processed agrifood. Country-specific reserves are for principal supplying interests only — no general FTA pool.

The upper end of your request (1.5Mt reserve, 2.2Mt pool) is refused — at that level the reserve approaches half of representative UK trade plus the FTA-partner claims of Turkey, Korea, India and Japan still to be accommodated, and the Council could not defend the regime's protective object. The red line is that it moves only with everything else, never alone, and the settlement confirmation we require is framed as finality of this matter, not renunciation of WTO rights.

It does not justify the upper end of your requested range: the UK is managing the threat as leverage precisely because it costs them nothing, their own analysts will tell them a failed negotiation damages their industry more than ours, and overpaying for coalition-avoidance invites Turkey, Korea, India and Japan to price the same threat in their own tracks. Settle within mandate; do not chase the threat.

private_rationale: We are giving Geneva more than I would like and less than they asked, deliberately. The 1.2Mt reserve ceiling is my genuine walk-away: above it, member states with steel production will not vote the package in June and the regime loses its protective rationale; below the UK walking, we take the 400,000t default, absorb UK retaliation against our 3.6Mt of exports, and blame UK maximalism — our analysts say no-deal hurts them more, and their Round 3 tone ('bridgeable', 'one round left') suggests they know it. The disapplication provision was always more valuable as a bargaining chip than as law; folding it into equivalence lets the UK claim a structural win while we keep the substance. If the UK rejects the final package, the record must show a substantially equivalent EU offer on the table; that record is our defence against both their withdrawal of concessions and any dispute.
